CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing retaliatory tariffs in place and reopen talks aimed at freezing the 1 January 2019 step-up of List 3 from 10% to 25%, without offering structural industrial-policy concessions or a large new purchase package until Washington can lock in a durable bargain. Do not add tariffs or non-tariff measures now: the White House has already threatened a further ~$267B “phase three” list if we escalate, and we have already used most of the US export base available for proportional retaliation. Use the window through the US midterms to test a freeze-and-talk path; if that channel fails, hold the current posture rather than concede.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential. Combined Section 301 coverage is now ~$250B of Chinese exports (Lists 1–2 at 25%; List 3 at 10% since 24 September, scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 January), and the US has demonstrated firm-level tech coercion (ZTE component ban; NDAA bar on Huawei/ZTE in US government systems). The yuan has fallen from about 6.32 in late April to 6.93 on 17 October (~9.7%), FX reserves slipped about 1.8% to $3.07T, and Chinese equities are in a bear market even after a fourth RRR cut. That maps to the high-threat CHN anchor (major export hit, FX pressure, national-champion targeting). It is not existential: industrial production is still ~5.9% YoY, seasonally adjusted merchandise exports are holding, and reserves remain above $3T. Further escalation is the wrong response to this threat. We already matched the $50B lists and then put 5–10% on ~$60B of US goods; another tariff or rare-earth/firm-harassment move would likely trigger List 4 and worsen FX and equity stress. Unilateral purchase concessions already failed in May (joint statement, then the White House proceeded with 301 ten days later). Therefore negotiate without new commitments: seek to stop the January step-up and reopen a channel, while preserving current leverage and accelerating domestic tech substitution.
key_factors: US Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese exports; List 3 is scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on 1 Jan 2019
Trump has threatened a further ~$267B list covering remaining Chinese exports if China escalates again
Yuan down ~9.7% since April and approaching 7.0; reserves down ~1.8% to $3.07T; A-shares in a bear market
May 19 purchase-heavy truce collapsed on 29 May — purchase-only deals are not durable against US structural/IP demands
Firm-level tech coercion (ZTE denial order; NDAA Huawei/ZTE government ban) hits Made in China 2025 more than tariffs alone
China has already exhausted most proportional tariff ammunition on US goods; US real economy still strong (Fed hiking, high sentiment)
Industrial production and aggregate Chinese exports have not broken — threat is high, not existential

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
China industrial production still expanding: 105.9 in Oct (same period previous year = 100), modest slowdown from 106.8 in May.
If China does retaliate, the President’s statement says that the Administration “will immediately pursue phase three, which is tariffs on approximately $267 billion of additional imports.”
Trump signs NDAA measure banning US government and contractors from using Huawei and ZTE components, effective over the next two years.
PBOC signalled it was not comfortable with further yuan losses and managed to steady the currency before it tested the sensitive 7-per-dollar level.
